html:
Congo is the name the map gives to the land north of the lower Congo River from 1492 to the present: first the realm of the Kingdom of Kongo and its neighbours, then French Congo, and since 1960 the Republic of the Congo, with its capital at Brazzaville.

The name comes from the Kongo people. Their kingdom, ruled from Mbanza Kongo south of the river, was at its height when the Portuguese arrived in 1483. Its king was baptised in 1491, and Afonso I made Kongo a Catholic kingdom. North of the river, along the coast, lay the Kingdom of Loango, a major exporter of ivory, cloth and then enslaved people.

The Atlantic slave trade took a heavy toll on the whole region. Kongo broke up in civil wars after 1665, and the prophet Kimpa Vita tried to reunite it before she was burned in 1706.

In 1880 the explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza signed a treaty with the Teke king that gave France the north bank, where Brazzaville was founded. Concession companies forced people to gather rubber, and many died building the Congo-Ocean railway. The colony, called Middle Congo, was part of French Equatorial Africa, and Brazzaville was its capital.

The Republic of the Congo became independent in 1960. It was a Marxist one-party state from 1969 to 1991, fought civil wars in the 1990s, and has been ruled for most of the time since 1979 by Denis Sassou Nguesso. Oil is its main export.
